extracted.intended_audience: students, coaches, and problem-solvers preparing for math olympiads (China Girls' Mathematical Olympiad)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of contest problems and official solutions from the China Girls' Mathematical Olympiad (various years); includes problem statements, solution approaches, and remarks about typical methods (e.g., parity, inequalities, geometry, combinatorics). Useful as guidance for solving/constructing olympiad-level contest solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition format / procedural requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The competition lasts for 2 days, and there are 4 problems to be completed within 4 hours each day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies time allotment and number of problems per day; affects strategies for time management and problem selection during the contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended problem approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem (1) is an open-ended problem. It asks whether there is an arrangement satisfying the requirement above. If an arrangement exists, we must construct a concrete example (see the example we have given). If not, we will prove it. (It is usually proved by contradiction.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For open-ended existence questions, either provide an explicit construction or prove impossibility—common technique: assume existence and derive contradiction. Also check small cases and provide explicit examples when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity reduction in divisibility problems
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy to see that n is an even number. Let n = 2m, then ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common start: determine parity of unknowns, substitute n=2m (or similar) to simplify divisibility conditions; then manipulate to get bounds or congruences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility bounding and modular decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform expressions (e.g., 2003m+1001 = 100(20m+1) + 3m+901), then deduce divisibility relations like 20m+1 | 3m+901.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite large linear combinations to isolate multiples of candidate divisors, deduce congruences or bounds, then test finite small cases as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing / combinatorial counting for duty schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: Since she is on duty just one time with every one of other girl students, and three people are on duty every day. So all other girl students can be paired up two by two. Hence 2 | 3n-1, therefore n is an odd number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial counting/pairing arguments to deduce parity or cardinality constraints in scheduling/design problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality technique: expand squares to get bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: From (a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2 ≥ 0, we get a^2 + b^2 + c^2 ≥ ab + bc + ca, so K > 5. Hence K > 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic identities (sum of squares) to produce inequalities comparing symmetric sums; useful to bound constants or ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test extremal/configuration examples for sharpness
rubrics_metrics.description: Since there is no triangle with sides 1,1,2 respectively, by the assumption in the problem we have ... that is, K < 6. We will prove that K = 6 satisfies the requirement below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check degenerate/extreme numeric configurations (e.g., 1,1,2) to obtain necessary bounds; then verify candidate values achieve the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sine rule, circumradius and trig identities in geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: DE = c cos C, DF = b cos B; using R (circumradius) and sin2θ identities we derive DE+DF = 2R sinA cos(B-C) = a cos(B-C) < a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate segment lengths to side lengths via sine rule and trig identities; express sums in terms of circumradius R and angles to obtain inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent-secant theorem and cyclic-quadrilateral arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Using tangent–secant theorem: AC^2 = AE * AB; and showing points A,F,D,E are concyclic leads to AH * AD = AC^2, establishing proportional equalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cyclicity and apply tangent–secant or power-of-a-point results to relate products of segment lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection/permutation counting via lines through a point
rubrics_metrics.description: For projections of points onto directed lines, only directed lines through a fixed point 0 need be discussed; lines perpendicular to point-pair joinings cause coincident projections and do not produce permutations. The number of distinct permutations equals 2K where K is the number of perpendiculars from 0 to lines joining point pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count permutations by analyzing critical directions (perpendiculars) and partitioning circle of directions into intervals where ordering is constant; multiply by 2 for orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry/virtual-element trick for permutation-sum invariants
rubrics_metrics.description: Add a virtual student A so that every seat is occupied by exactly one student. Denote S' the sum; note that exchanging adjacent students doesn't change S', and every student can return to original seat by adjacent exchanges, so S' = 0. Then S differs from S' by the virtual student's contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce a symmetric or virtual element to exploit invariance under adjacent swaps/permutations; reduces problem to checking a small set of extremal placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary representation / uniqueness for counting powers-of-two sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Each even nonnegative integer e less than 2004 can be written uniquely in the form e = Σ_{i=1}^{10} a_i 2^i where a_i = 0 or 1 (binary representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit binary expansion uniqueness to biject combinatorial choices with integer partitions into powers of two; useful in counting subset-sum type problems with powers of two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating-function coefficient extraction for counting hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct generating function f(x) = (1+x)^2 (1+x^2)^{10} (1+x^4)^{10} (1+x^8)^{10} ... and extract coefficient [x^{2004}] f(x) to count hands with value 2004.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model combinatorial selection problems with generating functions; coefficient extraction gives counts, sometimes simplified by truncation if target < base exponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: AM-GM, Cauchy and classical inequalities for extremal bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AM-GM and Cauchy to derive u+v+w ≥ √3 for u,v,w positive reals with uv + vw + wu > 1; equality when u=v=w=1/√3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard inequality chain (AM-GM, Cauchy-Schwarz) and check equality conditions to determine maximal/minimal constants in inequality problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction and monotonicity for sequence lower bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Show sequence {a_n} is strictly increasing and bound growth by induction (e.g., a_{n+1} ≥ n a_1), to deduce a_{2004} > 1 and derive sum inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove monotonicity and use induction to get explicit lower bounds for later terms; substitute into sums to prove inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive arrangements and explicit permutations to prove existence
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a number is 'good' (exists permutation with ak + k is a perfect square for all k), provide explicit permutations for each candidate (examples provided for 13,15,17,19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit sequences/permutations demonstrating required property rather than abstract existence proofs; often small-case constructive examples suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal/combinatorial tiling and packing via partitioning into subboards
rubrics_metrics.description: To bound max number of non-overlapping crosses on a 10x11 board, consider centers restricted to 8x9 subboard, tile this into three 8x3 boards, then analyze max centers per 2x3 or 3x3 subboard and use parity/symmetry to exclude 16-center placements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition large combinatorial board into smaller subboards with known local maxima, use symmetry and local constraints to derive global upper bounds; provide constructions to achieve upper bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisor pairing via multiplicative last-digit properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prime factor p has last digit 3 or 7, write divisors as a_s p^t and pair a_s p^t with a_s p^{t±1} as a 'partner' whose last digit differs, showing at most half the divisors end in 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiplicative structure and behavior of last digits under multiplication by primes to set up injective pairing between divisors with certain last digits and partners without that last digit; yields cardinality bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cyclic quadrilateral and angle-chasing for concurrency/cyclicity proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Show points are concyclic by proving angle sums equal 180° via angle-chasing: e.g., LFEA = LCGA and LBH + LBEF = 180°, hence B, E, F, H concyclic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine known right angles, parallel lines, and cyclic angle equalities to establish cyclicity; use similar triangles where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement strategy for minimizing/maximizing neighbor-products on a circle
rubrics_metrics.description: For five nonnegative reals summing to 1, constructive arrangement (e.g., order them a>b>c>d>e and place them in a specific circular order) ensures neighboring products meet upper/lower bounds like ≤ 1/9 or ≥ 1/9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sorting and specific placements around the circle to force neighbor-product extremal values; combine with simple bounds (e.g., sum constraints) to prove the claim.
